transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2027-06-30 15:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Rivera (Redwood SE), Lena Park (HarborTek Head of AI), Owen Brooks (CTO), Nadia Velasquez (ML Engineer), Samir Gupta (Security)

Summary (auto-gen, optional): quick scoping call to understand HarborTek's model needs: heavy multimodal notes ingestion, long-context summarization, multilingual customer support, potential on-prem requirement for sensitive docs, evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private. Actionable next steps agreed.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood Inference, and with me is Diego, our SE. How are you all?
[00:05] Lena Park: Hi, thanks. Good. Excited to dig in — we have, uh, a few constraints to share.
[00:12] Diego Rivera: Awesome. Maybe quick agenda — model selection, context length, multilingual support, tool-calling for APIs and vector search, and then deployment options (hosted/dedicated/private) and security.
[00:18] Owen Brooks: Sounds good. We're trying to avoid re-architecting our stack — core ask: ingest long call transcripts (up to 80k tokens), combine with internal docs and images, and surface answers in multiple languages. We also need some tool integration to call our knowledge-base API and a ticketing system.
[00:32] Maya Chen: Great, that's super helpful. Quick clarifying Q: when you say 80k tokens is that worst-case or typical? And are images OCR'd first or do you need multimodal model that natively consumes images?
[00:44] Lena Park: Worst-case, about 80k tokens for concatenated context — like multi-session transcripts plus appendix. For images we have OCR pipeline but want to explore native multimodal for higher fidelity later.
[00:56] Nadia Velasquez: Also multilingual: Spanish and Portuguese support for customer responses, and some Japanese. Latency SLO is 500–800ms on 95p for short queries; for long summaries we can allow up to 8s.
[01:10] Diego Rivera: Okay, thanks. So from model perspective we typically recommend splitting by workload. For short conversational responses a family of 7–13B open models (quantized) on Hosted can hit low-latency; for long-context summarization (80k) you probably need models with extended context (100k+) — either native long-context models or windowing + retrieval + KV cache. Also we can run Redwood Dedicated with accelerated kernels if you need predictable throughput.
[01:33] Owen Brooks: What's the difference cost-wise? We're sensitive to per-token egress and also peak concurrency during business hours.
[01:40] Maya Chen: Short answer: Hosted is pay-as-you-go — good for prototyping and variable load. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and better per-token economics at scale, plus isolation. Private (VPC/on-prem) is enterprise-contract and price includes support and infra. We'll send a side-by-side later.
[01:53] Samir Gupta: On security, we require SOC2, SAML SSO, tenant-level audit logs, and KMS-managed keys. Any gaps?
[01:58] Diego Rivera: We support SOC2, SAML, RBAC, and HSM/KMS integrations for Private and Dedicated; hosted supports customer-controlled KMS in our managed offering. There are some small caveats but we'll put them in the security pack.
[02:10] (crosstalk)
[02:12] Lena Park: For tool-calling, we need the model to trigger two actions: call our vector search to retrieve docs, and then call a ticketing API to create/append tickets. Can Redwood handle function-calling or do we need separate orchestration?
[02:25] Diego Rivera: Yes, we support function/tool-calling patterns — you can configure allowed tool endpoints and use structured outputs. We recommend building a small middleware to validate calls and handle auth. In Dedicated/Private you can push that middleware inside the VPC.
[02:38] Owen Brooks: Are there any recommended open models for long context? We looked at several but it's messy.
[02:44] Maya Chen: For native long-context, candidates include LongLM variants and certain Llama-derivatives with extended context, as well as Mistral's longer context forks. Another pattern is segmenting with Retriever + RAG + KV cache; models such as Llama 2-70B or Falcon-180B fine-tuned for summarization can work with chunking. Diego?
[02:59] Diego Rivera: Yeah, and to add, quantization will change throughput. If you need 80k native context, the GPU memory and kernel choices matter — Dedicated lets us pick instances with large memory and optimized kernels. For Hosted we'll likely use a compatible long-context runtime but there may be concurrency limits.
[03:14] Nadia Velasquez: Do you have benchmarks for 80k summarization? Rough numbers, not super-precise.
[03:19] Diego Rivera: Sorry timestamp glitch. Benchmarks — for a 80k summarization on a 70B-class model we see generation time in the order of 6–20 seconds depending on sampling and if we precompute embedds; with Dedicated optimized runtimes the lower end is reachable. Hosted might be 10–30s depending on queueing.
[03:33] Lena Park: That variance is big — we'll need predictable SLAs for batch nightly summarization jobs vs interactive queries.
[03:40] Maya Chen: We can propose Reserved Dedicated pools for nightly jobs and Hosted for interactive. Also you can define routing policies so critical latency queries use higher tier.
[03:49] Owen Brooks: On multilingual: do you recommend multilingual models vs ensemble of language-specific models?
[03:54] Diego Rivera: If you have heavy multi-lang support with similar volume, a single multilingual model simplifies ops. But for high quality in specific languages (Japanese, Portuguese) you might prefer specialized models or fine-tuning. Redwood supports per-request model routing.
[04:08] Samir Gupta: Data residency: Can we keep EU customer data in EU region? We need to ensure logs and cached embeddings remain in region.
[04:16] Maya Chen: Yes, region pinning is available in Dedicated and Private; for Hosted we have EU regions and can apply residency controls — embeddings cache residency can be configured. We'll include specifics in the security doc.
[04:26] (brief pause)
[04:30] Owen Brooks: What's involved in Private on-prem? We're curious but worried about ops overhead.
[04:34] Diego Rivera: Private is heavier upfront — you manage infra but Redwood provides control plane options and an on-prem package. It includes the runtime, orchestration, and connectors. We offer a transfer plan: start Hosted, move to Dedicated, then Private if needed.
[04:47] Nadia Velasquez: One technical Q: KV cache — is that persisted across restarts? We sometimes precompute conversation state.
[04:53] Diego Rivera: Yes, KV caches can be persisted to stateful volumes in Dedicated/Private. On Hosted we offer ephemeral caches with optional snapshot export.
[04:59] Lena Park: Regarding tool-calling security, can we whitelist tool endpoints and limit data exposure?
[05:05] Maya Chen: Absolutely — function calls are allowed only to configured endpoints and we support request/response inspection and masking. We'll document auth patterns.
[05:12] Owen Brooks: Any gotchas with embeddings? We need high recall for our KB.
[05:16] Diego Rivera: Embedding model choice matters; smaller vectors are cheaper but may lose recall. We can A/B test; Redwood Optimize can recommend which embedding model and dimensionality fits tradeoffs.
[05:28] (some ambient typing / background noise)
[05:32] Lena Park: Ok, practical: what do you need from us to run a pilot?
[05:36] Maya Chen: Ideally a representative doc set (5–10GB), sample prompts across languages, traffic profile (qps, concurrency), and security requirements. We'll provision a small Dedicated trial or run hosted benchmarks.
[05:46] Owen Brooks: We're ok with sending a sanitized 4GB corpus and some synthetic Spanish/Portuguese prompts.
[05:50] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll also set up a test slack channel and share our benchmark harness. Diego will own the run.
[05:57] Diego Rivera: Yep — I'll create a reproducible harness and include instructions to reproduce locally. We'll run hosted first, then a Dedicated sizing estimate.
[06:06] Samir Gupta: Please make sure the security pack includes KMS details, SOC2/ISO status, and data deletion policies.
[06:12] Maya Chen: Will do.
[06:14] (quick wrap)
[06:15] Maya Chen: Recap: HarborTek to provide corpus + sample prompts by July 5; Maya to send pricing, SOC2 pack, and region residency docs by July 2; Diego to run hosted benchmark and return results by July 6; schedule SE deep-dive week of July 12. Any objections?
[06:30] Owen Brooks: No objections. Sounds good.
[06:33] Lena Park: Thanks, appreciate the clear plan.
[06:36] Maya Chen: Great, thanks all. We'll follow up in email and slack. Bye!
[06:40] (meeting ends)

Notes/Artifacts referenced: Benchmark harness link: https://redwood.example.com/bench/harbortek-2027; Security pack (shared): link to internal docs; Pricing spreadsheet: redacted link
